b: The title of Hossein Keshavarz and Maryam Ataei’s The Friend’s House Is Here evokes that of Abbas Kiarostami’s 1987 classic Where Is the Friend’s House? On the surface, the two films don’t seem to share much beyond their titles, as one follows a schoolboy in rural Iran, the other a pair of women working within Tehran’s underground art scene. But just as Kiarostami’s eight-year-old Ahmad is so devoted to his classmate that he risks his safety to return a notebook he mistakenly took home, the two leads of Keshavarz and Ataei’s film share a bond that’s tested when Iran’s theocratic regime detains one of them.

Pari (Mahshad Bahraminejad) and Hana (Hana Mana) live together in Tehran. The former is a theater director who works at an art gallery to pay the bills, while the latter is a dancer who’s amassed a sizable social media following. Much of the film’s first half follows their daily lives, and it quickly becomes apparent how different their personalities are: Pari is serious and focused, Hana flighty and carefree. (Their hairstyles—Pari’s straight and black, Hana’s curly and blond—offer a concise visual shorthand for their characters.) And yet a core of female camaraderie binds them together—so much so that when Pari’s underground artistic activities are discovered and she’s arrested, Hana, who’s just been approved for a visa to France, seriously considers canceling her plane ticket to stay behind and help her friend.

The Friend’s House Is Here certainly has topical, ethnographic value. Despite the government’s restrictions on speech and dress, the younger generation, according to the film, is determined to live as freely as it possibly can under the circumstances. (According to interviews the directors gave after the film’s Sundance premiere, the cast, many of them nonprofessional actors, and the crew shot it in secret.) Were it not for the occasional passing older adult imploring Pari and Hana to wear hijabs in public, their lives could be seen as a less raunchy version of the exploits of the central female quartet of Girls. Hana, for instance, has a boyfriend, Ali (Farzad Karen), whom she keeps at arm’s length emotionally because of her potential move to France.

To some degree, Keshavarz and Ataei reflect this youthful energy in their filmmaking. Many of the scenes featuring Pari and Hana together, at home or out in the world, are given a choppy, impulsive rhythm in Keshavarz’s editing, the quick shots highlighting privileged moments of intimacy between the two. Elsewhere, the filmmakers capture many dialogue scenes in long takes, with cinematographer Ali Ehsani’s camera slowly panning back and forth between characters—a stylistic trait that also suggests the abiding influence of Kiarostami.

Those unbroken long takes pay off most powerfully in the scene that serves as the fulcrum between the film’s two tonally discordant halves. When, after one of Pari’s theater performances, an audience member engages her in conversation and gradually reveals himself to be an agent cracking down on perceived anti-government expression, the camera’s slow, steady zoom into Pari’s increasingly terrified face is made all the more harrowing by the fact that, up to this point, the film hasn’t cut away from her a single time.

From there, The Friend’s House Is Here details Hana’s eventually successful attempt to raise enough bail money to get Pari released from prison, and the fallout that ensues. After the two retreat to a seaside village to stay with Pari’s mother (Zohreh Piran, Ataei’s aunt in real life), a stretch of the film’s second half follows the mother as she goes around town asking friends and acquaintances for money to repay Hana—a ritual that eventually leads her to sit her daughter down and desperately implore her to put her underground activities aside, at least for now. With Hana still intent on moving to France, the sense that the ordeal may have done lasting, perhaps irreparable, damage to Pari’s psyche is nothing short of devastating.

Ultimately, though, Keshavarz and Ataei’s perspective is one of cautious optimism, in which the bonds of friendship and the overriding need for self-expression win out over despair. The recent fates of veteran Iranian filmmakers like Jafar Panahi and Mohammad Rasoulof—the former was sentenced in October to an additional five years and one month in prison—suggest that such a perspective may verge on the idealistic. Still, The Friend’s House Is Here is nuanced enough, and its portrait of the two friends at its heart vibrant enough, to make that idealism feel hard-won and bittersweet rather than like so much naïve wishful thinking.

Cast: Mahshad Bahraminejad, Hana Mana, Farzad Karen, Zohreh Piran Director: Hossein Keshavarz, Maryam Ataei Screenwriter: Hossein Keshavarz, Maryam Ataei Distributor: Greenwich Entertainment Running Time: 97 min Year: 2026
